qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture ten. Concept drift detection. How a model notices that the world has changed.
A grocery app suggests plant milk to its shoppers.
A grocery app suggests plant milk to its shoppers.
In week one, the model learns who tends to click.
The model learns who clicks in week 1.
Week by week, the same shoppers click more and more often.
Week by week, the same shoppers click more often.
Shoppers aged thirty to forty-four now click forty-six percent of the time. The model still says twenty.
Ages 30–44: 46% click now. The model still says 20%.
The inputs are the same, but the rule behind them has changed. That is concept drift.
Same inputs, new rule: that is concept drift.
Each tick is one prediction. The tall red ticks are mistakes.
Each tick is one prediction. Tall red ticks are errors.
Abrupt drift is like a pandemic. Overnight, errors jump from ten to fifty percent.
Abrupt, like a pandemic: errors jump from 10% to 50%.
Gradual drift is like a slow economic change. The new rule creeps in bit by bit.
Gradual, like economic change: the new rule creeps in.
Recurring drift is like the seasons. The old rule comes back again and again.
Recurring, like the seasons: the old rule comes back.
The model never changed. The world did.
The model never changed. The world did.
Here are two models. One is frozen, and one retrains every four weeks.
One model is frozen; one retrains every 4 weeks.
In week six, the shoppers change their habits overnight.
Week 6: shoppers change habit overnight.
Retrained on weeks five to eight, the second model is still twenty percent wrong.
Retrained on weeks 5–8, it is still 20% wrong.
Only after week twelve is it back down to ten percent.
Only after week 12 is it back to 10%.
The frozen model stays stuck at fifty percent, because it never updates.
The frozen model stays at 50%: it never updates.
Each prediction becomes a one if wrong, a zero if right.
Each prediction becomes a 1 if wrong, a 0 if right.
Average those errors over a window of recent records.
Average the errors over a window of recent records.
The last ten hits thirty percent before any drift. A false alarm.
Last 10 hits 30% before any drift: a false alarm.
After the drift at record one hundred, it reacts within six records.
After the drift at record 100, it reacts by 106.
The last hundred and fifty is steady, but slow to reach thirty percent.
Last 150 is steady, but reaches 30% only at 174.
Too short is jumpy. Too long is slow.
Too short is jumpy, too long is slow.
Ad-win keeps a window of the most recent records.
ADWIN keeps a window of the most recent records.
While nothing changes, the window grows.
Nothing changes, so the window keeps growing.
Then a drift starts, and errors bunch up.
A drift at record 250: errors bunch up.
Now the old and new parts disagree, so ad-win cuts the forty oldest records.
Record 296: its parts disagree. Cut the 40 oldest.
It keeps cutting, down to a hundred and twenty-five.
It keeps cutting: 125 records left at record 334.
Once things are calm, the window grows again.
Calm again, so the window grows again.
A window of eighty records, about ten percent errors.
A window of 80 records, about 10% errors.
Ad-win tries every split, into an older part and a newer part.
ADWIN tries splits: an older part and a newer part.
With few new records, the gap is below the threshold. No cut.
Few new records: gap 0.55, threshold 0.79. No cut.
As records arrive, the threshold falls.
More records, a lower threshold.
Now the gap beats the threshold.
111 records: gap 0.54 beats the threshold 0.52.
So ad-win drops the eight oldest records. After that, no split passes.
Cut: drop the 8 oldest records. No split passes the test now.
Small parts need a big gap, so noise rarely causes a cut.
Small parts need a big gap, so noise rarely cuts.
D D M reads the errors. Ten of a hundred records are wrong.
DDM reads the errors: 100 records, 10 of them wrong.
So the error rate, p, is zero point one.
Error rate p = 10 ÷ 100 = 0.1.
The spread, s, is zero point zero three.
With four times the records, the spread halves.
Four times the records: s halves to 0.015.
D D M watches p plus s.
DDM watches p + s: the error rate plus its spread.
D D M plots p plus s as each record arrives.
DDM plots p + s as each record arrives.
The warning line is two spreads above the best moment. The change line is three.
Warning at p min + 2 s min, change at p min + 3 s min.
The best moment came at record one hundred and fourteen.
p min and s min: the best moment so far, record 114.
Soon after, every other prediction is wrong.
After record 121, every other prediction is wrong.
At record one hundred and twenty-eight, it crosses the warning line, and new records are stored.
Record 128: past the warning line. Store new records.
Ten records later, it crosses the change line. Drift detected.
Record 138: past the change line. Drift detected.
A new model is trained on the stored records.
Train a new model on records 128 to 138.
E D D M watches the gaps between errors: nine, twelve, eight, eleven, ten.
EDDM measures the gaps between errors: 9, 12, 8, 11, 10.
Its best score so far is twelve point eight.
Mean gap plus 2 spreads: 12.8, the best so far.
After a drift, the gaps shrink to twos and threes.
After a drift the gaps shrink: 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 2, 3.
Now the score is four point one, a ratio of zero point three two.
4.1 against the best 12.8: a ratio of 0.32.
Below zero point nine five is a warning. Below zero point nine is a drift.
Below 0.95 is a warning, below 0.90 a drift.
On a gradual drift, E D D M was thirty records faster than D D M.
Gradual drift: EDDM caught it after 108 records, DDM 138.
Drift can be abrupt, gradual or recurring, and it always shows up in the errors.
Ad-win grows its window while things are calm, and cuts it when the old and new parts disagree.
D D M warns, then signals a change, as p plus s climbs above its best.
